title: A set-membership answer that fits in a BLOB
description: Build a probabilistic set-membership filter from a column, ship it as a small `BLOB`, and probe it from anywhere DuckDB runs. Answer **"is this maybe in the set?"** in O(1) using a fraction of the memory of the source set — with **no false negatives** and a tunable false-positive rate. The classic use is *skipping work when the answer is definitely no*: pre-filter joins, skip partitions, dodge cache misses.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: Bitfilters materializes five families of [approximate-membership-query (AMQ) data structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximate_membership_query_filter) as DuckDB aggregate functions. Build the filter once, store the BLOB as an ordinary column, probe it later — locally, in another DuckDB instance, or shipped over the network.

bulletPoints.label: Skip a join when the answer is definitely no
bulletPoints.description: Build a filter from the small "interesting" side of a join, then test the large side against it. False positives let an unwanted row through; false negatives never happen — so the cheap probe + expensive verify pattern is exact for correctness.

bulletPoints.label: Per-partition data skipping
bulletPoints.description: Materialize one filter per logical partition, store alongside metadata, and probe at query time to skip whole partitions that can't possibly contain the key. For high-cardinality lookups against fact tables this routinely skips 99%+ of partitions.

bulletPoints.label: Compact set artifacts
bulletPoints.description: A [Binary Fuse 8](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08258) filter is under 9 bits per key — three orders of magnitude smaller than the source set for typical UUID workloads. Persist it in a Parquet column, ship it to another process, embed it in a manifest.

bulletPoints.label: Parquet-compatible Bloom filters
bulletPoints.description: `bloom_filter` builds the split block Bloom filter Parquet uses — for the same values and sizing it is byte-for-byte the filter DuckDB writes into Parquet files.

bulletPoints.label: DuckDB-native join filters
bulletPoints.description: One family emits filters in the same internal format DuckDB uses for its own runtime join filters — persist a filter, then re-use it in custom data-skipping logic the optimizer recognizes.

sections.title: Filter families
sections.description: Five families, each with its own design point. Pick on **how the filter is built and combined**, **memory**, and **false-positive rate** in that order — not the other way around.

bulletPoints.label: Quotient — mergeable, self-sizing option
bulletPoints.description: Merge per-partition filters into one with `quotient_filter(q, r, filter)`, or let `quotient_filter(r, value)` choose the slot count for you. Tunable slot count and FPR (~2^−r). See [Quotient filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient_filter).

bulletPoints.label: XOR — static, compact
bulletPoints.description: ~9 bits per key at ~0.39% FPR (8-bit) or ~18 bits per key at ~0.0015% FPR (16-bit) — about 20% smaller than a Bloom at the same FPR. Built once, queried many times. See the [Xor filters paper (Graf & Lemire, 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08258).

bulletPoints.label: Binary Fuse — smallest, build-once
bulletPoints.description: Typically lands under 9 bits per key with very fast construction and lookups — currently the most space-efficient static filter family. Default choice for read-heavy sets you build once.

bulletPoints.label: Bloom — incremental, mergeable, Parquet-compatible
bulletPoints.description: `bloom_filter` builds a split block [Bloom filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom_filter) sized for an expected number of distinct values and a target FPR. Merge filters with `bloom_filter_merge`; it never gets "full" — past its sizing the FPR just degrades gradually. Byte-for-byte the format DuckDB writes into Parquet files.

bulletPoints.label: DuckDB Bloom — native compatibility
bulletPoints.description: The `bitfilters_duckdb_*` functions speak DuckDB's internal Bloom filter format and hash layout, so a persisted filter slots into the engine's own data-skipping path.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: Every filter constructor is a DuckDB **aggregate function** that takes values of any type and returns a single `BLOB`. The result is dense, self-contained, and storable like any other column.

bulletPoints.label: Values go in, BLOBs come out
bulletPoints.description: Pass the column itself — `xor8_filter(email)`, no `hash()` needed. Values are hashed with XXH64 of a fixed byte encoding (the Parquet plain encoding where Parquet defines one, otherwise DuckDB's on-disk representation), which is deliberately stable across DuckDB versions — unlike DuckDB's `hash()`, which may change. `UBIGINT` values are used as keys exactly as given, for when you compute your own keys (e.g. with [`hashfuncs`](/products/extensions/hashfuncs)). LIST, STRUCT, MAP, ARRAY, UNION and ENUM values are rejected — cast them to VARCHAR or compute a `UBIGINT` key.

bulletPoints.label: Filters as columns
bulletPoints.description: Every filter is just a `BLOB` that starts with a 16-byte header recording the filter type, how values were hashed and the value type. Store it in a regular column, persist to Parquet, send over the wire, hold in a CTE, partition by anything — probe it with its `*_contains` function or the generic `bitfilter_contains`, and inspect it with `bitfilter_info`.

bulletPoints.label: Building is charged to memory_limit
bulletPoints.description: Filter construction counts against DuckDB's `memory_limit` — you get an Out of Memory error rather than unbounded memory use, and grouped xor, binary fuse and self-sizing quotient filter builds spill to disk when they don't fit in memory.

bulletPoints.label: No false negatives, ever
bulletPoints.description: The filter never lies about absence: a `false` from a probe means the key is definitively not in the source set. False positives are bounded — measure them by probing known non-members and confirm the rate matches the family.

bulletPoints.label: Set-membership only — not cardinality
bulletPoints.description: Bitfilters answers **"is X in the set?"**. For cardinality estimation ("how many distinct items?") and set intersection sizes, use the sibling [`datasketches`](/products/extensions/datasketches) extension — it has Theta sketches and HyperLogLog for that workload. The two extensions cover complementary problems.

sections.title: Honest limitations
sections.description: What probabilistic filters cannot do — read this before designing a system around one.

bulletPoints.label: False positives are inherent
bulletPoints.description: Every family here trades exactness for memory. A `true` from `*_contains` means *probably present*, not *definitely present*. If your downstream cannot tolerate even one wrong yes, pair the probe with an exact verify — the filter just narrows the candidate set.

bulletPoints.label: Filters cannot enumerate
bulletPoints.description: There's no way to list the members from a filter — it's set-membership only. If you need the elements themselves, store them; if you need cardinality, use [`datasketches`](/products/extensions/datasketches).

bulletPoints.label: XOR and Binary Fuse filters are build-once
bulletPoints.description: XOR and Binary Fuse filters are built once and immutable — adding a key requires a full rebuild, and they can't be merged. When the set grows over time, use `bloom_filter` (merge with `bloom_filter_merge`) or `quotient_filter` (merge with `quotient_filter(q, r, filter)`), or rebuild on a cadence that matches your write throughput.

bulletPoints.label: Tiny sets don't earn the filter
bulletPoints.description: For a few thousand elements an in-memory hash set or a sorted array is faster and exact. Bitfilters earns its keep when the source set is large enough that **storing the full set is what hurts** — millions of keys, per-partition replication, network ship costs.

bulletPoints.label: Quotient filters have a hard capacity
bulletPoints.description: A Quotient filter holds at most 2^q − 1 values and errors when full. A merge can grow `q` only by giving up as many remainder bits, so merging `(16, 8)` filters gives `(20, 4)`, not `(20, 8)`. Use `quotient_filter(r, value)` to size a filter to its input.

bulletPoints.label: New filter format
bulletPoints.description: Filters now carry a 16-byte header, so they are 16 bytes larger and older versions of the extension can't read them. BLOBs written by older versions are still read by the type-specific functions (e.g. `xor8_filter_contains`), but not by the generic `bitfilter_*` ones.

useCases.title: Pre-filter an expensive join or lookup
useCases.description: Build a filter from the small side, probe from the large side, verify only candidates that pass. The probe is O(1) and fits in cache; the verify only runs at the false-positive rate. Net: the join sees a fraction of the rows it would otherwise.

useCases.title: Per-partition data skipping
useCases.description: Materialize one Binary Fuse filter per partition at write time, store alongside partition metadata. At query time the probe tells the planner which partitions can possibly contain the key — skip the rest.

useCases.title: Ship a set as a tiny artifact
useCases.description: A 10M-key Binary Fuse 8 filter is ~11 MB. Persist it to S3, attach it to a manifest, distribute it to read replicas, embed it in a CDN — any place where shipping the full set would be too big.

useCases.title: Dedupe pre-check / cache hit prediction
useCases.description: Probe a filter built from "already-seen" keys before doing the expensive dedupe work. Misses are free; hits go to the exact path. Same pattern for predicting cache hits before issuing the round-trip.
